query_context: Comprehensive global geopolitical update — 39 countries across conflict zones, major powers, and regional actors. Compiled from four research groups covering Middle East, Europe/Asia, Africa, and global powers.

events.summary: On Day 17 of the Israel-Iran war (March 16, 2026), the IDF struck Mehrabad International Airport in Tehran, destroying an aircraft that had served late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior regime officials. Israeli forces declared they would continue targeting any assets used by Iranian military forces throughout Iran. Smoke and fires were visible at the airport following the strikes.

Israel's Defense Minister Israel Katz announced the beginning of a 'ground maneuver' in southern Lebanon on March 16, escalating the conflict with Hezbollah beyond airstrikes. Parts of the 91st Division moved into areas around the strategic town of Khiam, which sits on high ground near the Litani River and commands views over northern Israel. Israel stated the goal was to push Hezbollah north and dismantle its weapons infrastructure south of the Litani River.

Israel launched a 'broad wave' of strikes across western and central Iran on March 15, hitting over 200 targets including IRGC command centers manned by Iranian soldiers, air defense systems, and weapon storage and production sites. The IDF stated it still had 'thousands of targets' remaining in Iran, with new ones identified every day. Strikes also targeted the Hamedan area, hitting several IRGC and Basij headquarters.

The IDF reported by March 15 that approximately 70–75% of Iran's ballistic missile launchers had been destroyed since the start of the war, up from 60% earlier in the week. The IDF had struck key production sites in Parchin and Shahrud, targeting factories producing explosive materials for warheads, missile engine facilities, and advanced cruise missile R&D complexes. Iran's daily missile fire rate dropped from approximately 95 on Day 1 to fewer than 15 by mid-conflict.

Israel is planning a massive ground invasion of southern Lebanon, aiming to seize the entire area south of the Litani River, according to US and Israeli officials cited by Axios on March 14. The operation was triggered after Hezbollah fired over 200 rockets at northern Israel on March 12 in coordination with an Iranian missile barrage. A senior Israeli official stated: 'Before this attack we were ready for a ceasefire in Lebanon, but after it there is no way back from a massive operation.'

relationships.summary: Active full-scale war since February 28, 2026 (Day 17 as of March 16). Joint US-Israeli Operation Epic Fury/Roaring Lion has struck 5,000+ targets inside Iran. Israel has destroyed 70%+ of Iran's missile launchers, struck nuclear sites at Natanz, and targeted the Supreme Leader's aircraft. Iran has retaliated with daily ballistic missile barrages against Israeli cities.

Active war with Hezbollah since March 2, 2026. Israel launched ground operations in southern Lebanon on March 16. Over 850 killed in Lebanon and 800,000+ displaced. IDF has struck 500+ Hezbollah targets including Beirut command centers, financial institutions, and killed multiple senior Hezbollah and IRGC commanders operating in Lebanon.

Joint Operation Epic Fury/Roaring Lion with full US military backing. US provides air assets, intelligence, and diplomatic cover. Trump administration supports Israeli ground action in Lebanon and continues strikes on Iranian targets. Trump has called on NATO allies and China to send warships to keep Strait of Hormuz open.

Gaza ceasefire Phase 2 is in effect since October 2025, but Israel closed all Gaza crossings on February 28 when the Iran war began, triggering a humanitarian crisis. IDF continues limited strikes in Gaza. The West Bank faces increased checkpoint closures and settler violence.

Israel continues to maintain military presence in southern Syria and conducts periodic strikes. Israeli incursions into Quneitra were reported in early March 2026. Israeli air defenses intercepted Iranian drones over Syrian territory. Both sides describe deployments as defensive.

events.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi declared on March 16 that the Strait of Hormuz is 'accessible, but restricted to our adversaries' and rejected Trump's claim that Iran was seeking a ceasefire, stating 'We have never requested a ceasefire, nor have we sought negotiations.' Araghchi said Iran is 'prepared to defend ourselves for as long as necessary,' while simultaneously telling Al-Araby al-Jadeed that Iran is ready to consider any proposal that includes 'a complete end' to the war.

Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his assassinated father on March 4 after a contentious week-long succession battle within the Assembly of Experts, issued his first written statement on March 13 vowing to keep the Strait of Hormuz closed and threatening all US military bases in the region. The NYT reported on March 16 that the succession involved intense rivalry between the Khamenei and Khomeini dynasties, with IRGC generals playing a decisive role in securing Mojtaba's 59 of 88 votes.

Reports emerged on March 15 that new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei was secretly flown to Moscow for life-saving leg surgery after being badly wounded in a drone strike, according to Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Jarida citing a high-ranking source. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed on March 13 that Khamenei was 'wounded and likely disfigured,' noting his first public statement came only in written form without any audio or video. As of March 16 Khamenei has not been seen in public since his appointment.

Iran's UN representative reported to the Security Council that at least 1,348 civilians have been killed in Iran since the war began on February 28. Iran's Health Ministry confirmed 223 women and 202 children are among the dead. The International Committee of the Red Cross placed the death toll at over 1,300. Iranian missile fire has continued daily though at a drastically reduced rate from 95 missiles on Day 1 to fewer than 15 per day by mid-conflict.

US and Israeli forces struck the Natanz nuclear facility entrance buildings on March 2-3, confirmed by the IAEA, though the agency said there were no radiological effects. The IDF also struck Iran's main ballistic missile production sites at Parchin and Shahrud, factories producing explosive materials for warheads, and the IRGC's Imam Hossein University used for officer training. More than 600 regime targets were struck using approximately 2,500 munitions in the first days alone.

relationships.summary: Active full-scale war since February 28 after Israel-US joint strikes assassinated Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and degraded Iran's military infrastructure. Iran has fired 200+ ballistic missiles at Israel. Israel has struck 5,000+ targets inside Iran including nuclear sites, missile production facilities, and regime command centers.

Iran backs Hezbollah, which entered the war on March 2. Four senior IRGC Quds Force commanders were killed in an Israeli strike on Beirut's Ramada hotel on March 8. Iran directed Hezbollah's coordinated attack of 200+ rockets on March 12. Iran's ability to resupply Hezbollah is severely degraded with 16 Quds Force aircraft destroyed.

New Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei thanked the Houthis for their backing in his first statement and hinted they might soon enter the war. Houthis have declared 'fingers are on the trigger' but have not yet joined active combat, reportedly constrained by internal divisions, fear of leadership assassinations, and a May 2025 US-brokered ceasefire.

Iran-backed Iraqi militias including Kataib Hezbollah and the Islamic Resistance in Iraq have carried out daily drone and rocket attacks on US bases and the Baghdad embassy. Iran uses Iraqi territory as a proxy battleground. Six US service members died in an aircraft crash in western Iraq on March 12 during Operation Epic Fury.
Reports suggest Russia provided medical evacuation to Moscow for Mojtaba Khamenei's surgery in one of Putin's palaces. Russia has not intervened militarily but maintains strategic ties with Tehran.

events.summary: Israel officially announced 'focused ground operations' in southern Lebanon on March 16, with parts of the 91st Division entering territory around the strategic hilltop town of Khiam near the Litani River. Fighting intensified as Israeli forces sought to cut Hezbollah's supply lines and push the group further north from the Israeli border. The IDF's Defense Minister Katz framed it as the opening of a 'ground maneuver' with potential for significant expansion.

Lebanon's Health Ministry confirmed that 850 people had been killed since renewed fighting began on March 2, 2026, with approximately 850,000 people displaced — roughly 14% of Lebanon's entire population. The Lebanese government took the unprecedented step of proscribing Hezbollah's 'military and security' activities and ordered it to surrender its weapons to the state. Beirut also ordered the detention and deportation of any IRGC personnel operating in Lebanon.

An Israeli airstrike on a health center in Burj Qalaouiyah on March 13 killed 12 people — nearly the entire medical team of paramedics, doctors, and nurses — leaving only one severely injured survivor. Lebanon's Health Ministry condemned the attack as 'criminal conduct' and accused Israel of targeting medical personnel. The IDF simultaneously accused Hezbollah of making 'extensive military use' of ambulances and medical facilities as cover.

Israeli forces struck the Ramada hotel in central Beirut on March 8, killing four key IRGC Quds Force commanders who were planning terror attacks on Israel, with the IDF later confirming five total senior commanders from the Lebanon Corps of the Quds Force were eliminated. The IDF also eliminated the Hezbollah Radwan Force's southern Lebanon unit commander Abu Ali Riyan, with over 100 terrorists killed and more than 60 Radwan Force command centers dismantled since the conflict began.

By March 6, the IDF claimed to have struck over 500 Hezbollah targets throughout Lebanon and conducted 26 waves of airstrikes in the Dahiyeh area of Beirut alone. Strikes targeted Hezbollah's financial institution Al-Qard al-Hassan, with approximately 30 branches struck over the conflict's first week. IDF Chief of Staff Zamir declared the IDF 'will not desist until Hezbollah is disarmed.'

relationships.summary: Active war between Israel and Hezbollah since March 2, 2026. Israel launched ground operations in southern Lebanon on March 16. The Lebanese state has taken unprecedented steps to distance itself from Hezbollah, proscribing the group's military activities and ordering expulsion of IRGC personnel.

Lebanon's Hezbollah is Iran's primary proxy, entering the war to support Tehran on March 2. However, the Lebanese state itself has moved to expel IRGC personnel and disavow Hezbollah's military role. Iran's ability to resupply Hezbollah is severely degraded as Israeli strikes destroyed IRGC logistics aircraft.

Syria's new government reported that Hezbollah fired artillery shells into Syrian territory from Lebanon, landing west of Damascus. Syrian forces detected Hezbollah reinforcements at the Syrian-Lebanese border and issued warnings that such aggression would not be tolerated, representing a significant shift from Assad-era Syria-Hezbollah cooperation.

events.summary: The Strait of Hormuz closure has had a secondary economic effect on Syria, with Chatham House reporting that cargo formerly routed through Gulf waters is now being redirected overland through Syria and Jordan, making border crossings 'busier than they have been in years.' This represents an unexpected economic opportunity for Syria's transitional government amid the broader regional crisis.

Syria marked the 15th anniversary of its 2011 uprising on March 15, 2026, as the transitional government of President Ahmed al-Sharaa continued consolidating control over the country. Security challenges persist across multiple fronts: Israeli military presence in southern Syria, residual ISIS activity, and Hezbollah spillover from Lebanon. The government has been working to integrate Kurdish SDF forces following a January 30 comprehensive agreement brokered by the US.

The UN Syria Commission called in March 2026 for justice, reform, and international support, noting Syria's fragile transition remains undermined by ongoing violations. Israel has reportedly launched over 1,000 strikes against Syria and conducted 400+ ground incursions since December 2024 per Syrian President al-Sharaa's December 2025 Doha Forum statement. The UN Security Council in February 2026 welcomed the Damascus-SDF agreement and called for intensified counterterrorism cooperation against ISIS.

On March 10, the Syrian government and SDF carried out a prisoner exchange in Hasakah, releasing 100 detainees each, under the supervision of the presidential team implementing the January 30 agreement. Syrian Deputy Defense Minister Sipan Hamo (former YPG commander) was appointed to oversee military integration in the eastern region. The comprehensive SDF integration agreement includes gradual military/administrative merger, civil rights guarantees for Kurds, and border security cooperation.

Syria reinforced military deployments along its borders with Lebanon and Iraq in early March amid escalating regional tensions. Israeli air defenses intercepted over 10 Iranian drones over Daraa province, with debris falling in Ain Tarma near Damascus and Jaramana, causing minor injuries including to children. Syrian officials described their border reinforcements as defensive.

relationships.summary: Israel maintains military presence in southern Syria and continues periodic strikes. Over 1,000 Israeli strikes against Syria reported since December 2024. Syria's new government has sent 'messages of peace' but Israel has not withdrawn from occupied Syrian territory near the Golan. Both sides describe current posture as defensive.

Hezbollah artillery shells have landed in Syrian territory from Lebanon, provoking official Syrian warnings. Hezbollah reinforcements observed at Syrian-Lebanese border were met with Syrian military declarations it would not tolerate aggression — a dramatic shift from the Assad era when Hezbollah fought alongside Syrian forces.

Syria and Iraq are cooperating on border security and counterterrorism against ISIS. Transfer of 5,700 ISIS detainees from SDF-held Syrian prisons to Iraqi facilities in a US-led operation was completed in February 2026.

US forces have largely withdrawn from Syrian bases (al-Tanf, al-Shaddadi, Qasrak) in early 2026. US brokered the January 30 SDF-Damascus agreement. Trump held a call with al-Sharaa demanding cessation of fighting during the northeastern offensive. US killed or captured 50+ ISIS fighters and struck 100+ ISIS targets in Syria over two months.

events.summary: Iran's strategy of paralyzing the Strait of Hormuz was described by analysts as using the same blueprint the Houthis employed in the Red Sea in 2024, which reduced Red Sea container traffic by roughly 90%. The Houthis have announced they will resume attacks on ships in the Red Sea if regional dynamics warrant it, representing a conditional deterrence posture. Analysts from Al-Monitor warn Houthi involvement could extend the conflict to Saudi Arabia and UAE.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have remained on the sidelines of the active Iran war despite pressure to join. Houthi leader Abdulmalik al-Houthi has repeatedly declared 'our fingers are on the trigger' but no active military engagement has occurred as of March 16. New Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei publicly thanked the Houthis in his first statement and hinted they might soon open a new front, raising analysts' concerns about potential escalation.

Analysts at the Atlantic Council and Chatham House note that the Houthis are constrained from joining the Iran war by several factors: fear of leadership assassinations following high-profile killings elsewhere, internal divisions within Yemen, uncertainties over weapons supplies, and a May 2025 US-Oman-brokered ceasefire that paused their Red Sea campaign. The Chatham House notes the Houthis appear to be 'building up forces' and repositioning coastal missile batteries along Yemen's western coastline.

Reports in early March from Global Security Review described Houthi coastal entrenchment, with trench networks around Hodeidah and coastal missile positioning along Yemen's western coastline. AIS data shows vessel traffic through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb has resumed since the May 2025 ceasefire, but analysts warn the pause reflects strategic positioning rather than genuine de-escalation, and any Houthi reentry would immediately threaten rerouted tanker traffic.

relationships.summary: Iran's new Supreme Leader publicly thanked the Houthis and hinted at their imminent involvement in the war. Houthis remain the last major Iran-axis proxy not yet actively engaged. The Houthis maintain operational autonomy while their Red Sea campaign historically synchronized with broader Iranian-directed escalation cycles.

A May 2025 US-Oman-brokered ceasefire halted Houthi Red Sea attacks in exchange for suspension of US strikes on Yemen. The Houthis are currently respecting this ceasefire but analysts say involvement in the broader Iran war would likely trigger resumed US military action. Trump previously pledged to 'completely annihilate' the group.

The Houthis have expressed willingness to target Israel and Israeli-linked shipping but have not done so during the current conflict. Analysts note the Houthis 'hope to fight, especially with Israel, but can't be the ones to fire the first shot' given ceasefire constraints.

events.summary: Iraq's Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani faces mounting international criticism for his government's inability — or unwillingness — to stop Iranian-backed PMF militias from attacking American, French, Italian, and Kurdish military personnel and facilities. Fox News reported that 'the PMF are paid and armed by the Iraqi government' and 'are on the Iraqi payroll.' US and Israeli forces have also conducted retaliatory strikes targeting the PMF, placing Iraq at the center of the proxy conflict.

Five rockets struck Baghdad International Airport on the night of March 15, injuring four workers, according to the WSJ. Iran-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) militias have conducted daily drone and rocket attacks on US bases across Iraq, including over 300 drone and missile attacks on the Kurdistan Region since the start of Operation Epic Fury, killing seven people and injuring 35. A French soldier was killed by an Iranian-designed Shahed drone in Iraqi Kurdistan on March 14.

The US Embassy in Baghdad was struck by a missile on March 14, hitting the helipad within the heavily fortified Green Zone compound and damaging part of the embassy's air defense system. Kataib Hezbollah claimed responsibility. The attack was the second such strike on the embassy since the conflict began and prompted the US to immediately issue an emergency order for all American citizens to leave Iraq.

The US Embassy in Baghdad issued a Level 4 emergency security alert on March 14, ordering all American citizens in Iraq to 'leave immediately' due to 'Iran-aligned terrorist militias' attacking US personnel and facilities. The State Department stated 'Iran-aligned terrorist militias have attacked the International Zone in central Baghdad on multiple occasions.' This marked a dramatic escalation from a previous advisory issued the day prior simply to 'avoid conspicuous behavior.'

Six US service members were killed on March 12 when their aircraft crashed in western Iraq during Operation Epic Fury. US Central Command stated the aircraft was lost while flying over friendly airspace and the crash was 'not due to hostile fire or friendly fire.' Combined with earlier casualties from a March 1 Kuwait attack, the total US military death toll in the conflict reached 13.

relationships.summary: Iran-backed PMF militias integrated into Iraq's formal security structure conduct daily attacks on US interests. Iraq has become the primary proxy battleground for Iranian retaliation. Iran uses Iraqi territory for missile and drone launches against US bases across the region.

US ordered full evacuation of American citizens from Iraq on March 14 following repeated embassy and base attacks. 13 US service members killed in the conflict, including 6 in an Iraq aircraft crash. US/Israel conducting retaliatory strikes against Iranian-backed PMF groups inside Iraq. The US Embassy in Baghdad was struck twice since February 28.

Iraq cooperated with Syria and US-led coalition in transferring 5,700 ISIS detainees from Syrian SDF prisons to Iraqi facilities in a February 2026 operation. The two countries share concerns over ISIS resurgence amid regional instability.

events.summary: A Palestinian terror operative, Muhammad Majed Abd al-Salam Tawfiq Zidan, described as a 'key Palestinian terrorist who operated under the intelligence of the Iranian terror regime,' was killed in an IDF airstrike in Lebanon. The IDF stated Zidan was attempting to advance terror attacks against Israel. This illustrates the continued operational links between Palestinian armed groups and the Iranian axis during the broader regional war.

Al Jazeera reported on March 13 that since the Iran war began on February 28, Israel has maintained its military operations in Gaza despite global attention shifting to Iran. Since October 2023, over 72,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, predominantly women and children, with much of the territory destroyed. The Gaza ceasefire Phase 2 — covering demilitarization and reconstruction — was announced by the US on January 14, 2026, but its implementation remains deeply contested.

Israel closed all Gaza crossings on February 28, 2026 as the Iran war began, suspending entry of aid, fuel, commercial supplies, medical evacuations, and humanitarian staff rotations. This immediately triggered a humanitarian crisis in Gaza, where the electricity grid has been down since October 2023 and the population remains entirely dependent on external supplies. Limited crossings were partially reopened on March 3 after UN Secretary-General Guterres urgently called for access restoration.

The OCHA Humanitarian Situation Report of March 6 documented that sexual and reproductive health services in Gaza remain severely disrupted, with critical medical equipment such as ultrasound machines, incubators, and ventilators restricted as 'dual-use' items. Approximately 50,000 pregnant women are in Gaza with roughly 160-180 births daily. Food rations were reduced to 50% of minimum caloric needs in February, covering only 1.2 million people down from 1.6 million at full rations in January.

West Bank closures intensified sharply after February 28, with increased checkpoint closures severing movement between communities and governorates. Over 1,000 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli soldiers or settlers in the West Bank since October 2023. The UN reported nine incidents of ambulances being obstructed between February 28 and March 3, including vehicles held at gunpoint at checkpoints and medical teams forced onto longer routes.

relationships.summary: The Gaza ceasefire Phase 2 is nominally in effect since October 2025, but Israel closed all crossings when the Iran war began on February 28, triggering a renewed humanitarian crisis. Military operations continue in Gaza. The West Bank faces intensified closures and settler violence. Over 72,000 Palestinians killed in Gaza since October 2023.

Iran uses Palestinian armed groups as part of its 'axis of resistance.' Palestinian operatives have been identified operating under Iranian intelligence in Lebanon. Hamas remains nominally part of Iran's regional network despite the Gaza ceasefire, and Islamic Jihad maintains active Iranian backing.

Palestinian Islamic Jihad's Lebanon commander Adham Adnan al-Othman was killed in Beirut's southern suburbs during the conflict. Palestinian operatives have been identified as working with Hezbollah and IRGC intelligence networks in Lebanon.

events.summary: Russia launched a large-scale series of drone and missile strikes on March 13-14 that caused significant civilian casualties in Kyiv. Out of 137 drones launched by Russia, Ukraine's air force downed 122. Ukrainian President Zelensky stated that Russia is losing up to 35,000 soldiers a month and that Ukrainian forces have begun reclaiming territory for the first time since 2023.

President Zelensky told CNN that Russian intelligence suggests Russia provided Iran with drones used in Middle East strikes. Zelensky also condemned the US decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian oil already at sea, stating the move 'certainly does not contribute to peace.'

Ukraine recorded its first significant territorial gains since 2023, liberating parts of Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhia regions. Ukrainian forces recaptured nine towns in Zaporizhia since January and effectively cleared much of Russian presence in Dnipropetrovsk. Zelensky attributed the progress to Russia's mounting personnel losses and recruitment shortfalls.

US-brokered ceasefire talks between Russia and Ukraine were put on hold due to growing escalation in the Middle East. Both Russia and Ukraine claimed front-line progress, with Ukraine saying it pushed Moscow's forces back in Dnipropetrovsk and recaptured over 460 square kilometers of territory, while Russia claimed gains in Donbas. A Russian strike on Sloviansk killed four and wounded at least 16.

Russia signaled it would halt US-led peace negotiations unless Ukraine agreed to cede its eastern Donetsk region. Two Kremlin-close sources told Bloomberg that talks would be decisive, with Russia prepared to sign a peace memorandum only if Kyiv withdrew from Donetsk. The US had aimed for a March peace deal, but territorial disagreements and the Iran conflict have stalled progress.

relationships.summary: Active war ongoing since February 2022. Russia conducting near-daily missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities; Ukraine mounting counteroffensive operations and long-range strikes on Russian territory. US-brokered peace talks stalled as of March 2026 with both sides claiming battlefield gains.

US is the primary mediator of peace negotiations and a key military/financial supporter, though the Trump administration's temporary lifting of Russian oil sanctions and preoccupation with Iran has created friction. US-Ukraine negotiators discussed a May referendum framework.
Germany remains a strong supporter of Ukraine, with Chancellor Merz opposing any sanctions relief on Russia and affirming continued support for Ukraine despite the Middle East crisis.

Turkey has previously served as a mediator between Russia and Ukraine (2022 Istanbul talks). As a NATO member hosting the 2026 NATO Summit, Turkey maintains dialogue with both sides while balancing its own regional interests.

events.summary: Russian forces conducted a large-scale drone and missile strike campaign on March 13-14 targeting Kyiv and multiple Ukrainian oblasts, including Kharkiv, Mykolaiv, and Odesa. The ISW assessment noted Russia launched one Iskander-M missile and 126 drones. ISW's forecasts that economic pressure would force Kremlin concessions in 2026-2027 were undermined by the global oil price surge.

The US Treasury Department granted a temporary waiver allowing countries to buy sanctioned Russian oil already at sea until April 11, 2026. Russia's oil revenues surged as Urals crude prices rose approximately $30 per barrel amid the Iran crisis, adding an estimated $150 million+ in daily revenues. European allies condemned the US decision as a 'complete strategic error' that benefits Russia's war economy.

Russia's MVD (Interior Ministry) underwent leadership changes as Putin replaced its first deputy minister, signaling an internal security reshuffling. Putin also told Trump in a call that Russian forces were 'advancing rather successfully' in Ukraine, claiming Russia had reduced Ukraine's Donetsk control from 35% to 15-17%. Russia maintained standard condemnations of US-Israeli strikes on Iran without offering material support to Tehran.

Russia's oil and gas revenues fell 44% year-on-year in February 2026, and its fiscal deficit exceeded 90% of the full-year target before the Iran crisis. The global oil price shock reversed this deterioration, with Russian oil transforming from a 'global outcast' to high-demand commodity. Analysts projected Russia's budget could gain over $1.6 billion per month for every $10 increase in crude prices.

Belgian and French forces seized a Russian shadow-fleet oil tanker (Ethera) in Operation Blue Intruder, escorting it to the Port of Zeebrugge. France confirmed Navy helicopters participated. European nations have intensified operations against Russian shadow fleet vessels defying sanctions, even as the US has eased restrictions.

relationships.summary: Full-scale war ongoing. Russia continues near-daily strikes on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure while conducting offensive operations in Donbas and other regions. Peace talks remain stalled.

Nominally adversarial but interests have partially converged around the Iran crisis and oil markets. Trump administration temporarily lifted some Russian oil sanctions, which Moscow celebrated as a political vindication.

China is a key energy purchaser and diplomatic partner. The Iran crisis may deepen China's long-term reliance on Russian energy. Lavrov and Wang Yi coordinated on UNSC response to Middle East strikes.

Russia provided drones to Iran (per Zelensky's intelligence claims). Russia verbally condemned US-Israeli strikes on Iran but offered limited material support, constrained by its Ukraine commitments and desire for US concessions.

events.summary: Turkish NATO air defenses intercepted a third missile from Iran, and Turkey formally asked Tehran to clarify the incident. Turkey sits on NATO's southeastern flank bordering conflict zones, and its Patriot and S-400 systems are under heightened operational status amid the Iran-US-Israel conflict spillover.

NATO enhanced air defense systems in Turkey amid the Iran conflict spillover, with additional measures reinforcing Turkey's missile defense capabilities. Bloomberg reported Turkey's NATO defense posture is being further strengthened in response to the regional escalation, underscoring Turkey's frontline role as a NATO ally bordering the conflict zone.

President Erdogan spoke with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte about regional developments following the outbreak of the Iran war. Erdogan stressed that 'giving diplomacy a chance is important for achieving lasting peace' and confirmed preparations for the July 2026 NATO Summit in Ankara are continuing. Rutte affirmed NATO's commitment to 360-degree ally security.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan stated that Turkey is engaging all parties—including the US, Europeans, and Oman—to end the Iran war and resume diplomacy. Fidan warned that the Hormuz Strait closure 'could push the United States to obtain a quick result' and that the conflict risks engulfing the region. Erdogan separately condemned the US-Israeli attacks on Iran as a 'clear violation' of international law.

NATO announced in August 2025 that Turkey will host the 2026 NATO Summit at the Beştepe Presidential Compound in Ankara on July 7-8, 2026. This will be the second time Turkey hosts a NATO Summit, the first being Istanbul 2004. Turkey is also hosting COP31 in Antalya and the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States in 2026, marking a packed global diplomacy calendar.

relationships.summary: Turkey maintains complex relations with Russia — trading partner, energy buyer, and owner of Russian-made S-400 systems — while nominally opposing Russian aggression in Ukraine. Turkey has served as a mediator channel between Moscow and Kyiv.
Turkey has supplied Bayraktar TB2 drones to Ukraine and mediated grain deal negotiations. Turkey supports Ukraine's territorial integrity while maintaining back-channel communications with Russia.

Turkey shares a border with Iran, has economic ties, and is actively mediating to end the Iran war. Iran missiles have overflown or struck near Turkish territory, prompting diplomatic protests. Turkey seeks Iranian stability for its own energy and border security interests.

events.summary: Myanmar military continued intensive airstrikes in Chin State and Sagaing Division targeting resistance-held areas ahead of the new parliament's formation. Air strikes hit schools, churches, and homes, with military using the attacks as propaganda cover during Chin National Day celebrations. The Myanmar Peace Monitor recorded that military air assaults have killed at least 1,728 civilians over the past two years.

Myanmar's junta announced plans to form a five-member Union Consultative Council — a 'super-body' designed to give junta chief Min Aung Hlaing control over both the military and the incoming civilian-led government simultaneously. Legal experts warned this arrangement has no accountability mechanisms, effectively allowing Hlaing to assume the presidency while retaining full military command.

According to ACLED data, over 93,000 people have been killed due to violence in Myanmar since the 2021 coup, with nearly 4 million internally displaced. The UN estimates approximately 3.6 million displaced with 20 million requiring humanitarian assistance. Nineteen smaller armed resistance groups formed the Spring Revolution Alliance to coordinate the anti-junta armed struggle independently of the National Unity Government.

Myanmar's military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) won a dominant majority in the junta-run elections held across three phases (December 28, 2025 – January 25, 2026), capturing 232 of 263 lower house seats. The elections were condemned by ASEAN, the UN, and Western governments as fraudulent, designed to extend military rule. Voter turnout fell to approximately 55% as fighting prevented voting in 67 of 330 townships.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 documented that junta authorities have arrested over 30,000 people since the 2021 coup, with more than 2,200 dying in custody. In July 2025, the US lifted sanctions on junta allies involved in arms sales. Myanmar's humanitarian crisis deepened with the closure of 422+ health facilities due to funding cuts, and nearly half the population living in poverty.

relationships.summary: China is Myanmar's largest trading partner and arms supplier, and has blocked UN Security Council action against the junta. China backs the junta while also maintaining contacts with select ethnic armed groups along the border, particularly in Shan State, to protect its economic interests (pipelines, trade routes).

Russia is a major arms supplier to the Myanmar military, provides military advisers, and blocks UN Security Council action. Joint training programs and the Myanmar-Russia Joint Counter-Terrorism Committee (MRJCTC) have materially enhanced junta military capabilities.

The US has imposed sanctions on junta figures but in July 2025 lifted some sanctions on junta allies involved in arms sales. The US terminated Temporary Protected Status for Myanmar nationals in November 2025.

events.summary: On March 15, Pakistan launched fresh airstrikes on Kandahar targeting militant hideouts, while four civilians in Pakistan's Bajaur were killed by Taliban mortar fire. Afghanistan claimed to have struck an army camp in Pakistan's South Waziristan, reportedly destroying the command centre. The UN condemned the conflict and called for an immediate cessation of hostilities to allow humanitarian aid flow.

Pakistan launched multiple airstrikes targeting Kabul, Kandahar, and Paktia on March 13, 2026, as part of ongoing Operation Ghazab Lil Haq, which began on February 26-27. Pakistan claimed to have struck the headquarters of the Afghan Army's 313 Corps while the Taliban stated strikes caused civilian casualties. By March 13, Pakistani officials claimed 641 Taliban fighters killed and 855 injured since hostilities began.

The UN Security Council was briefed on March 9 that Afghanistan's humanitarian crisis is worsening due to the Pakistan conflict, the Iran war disrupting trade routes, and the closed Pakistan border. The 2026 humanitarian appeal of $1.71 billion is only 10% funded. Afghanistan has absorbed 5.5 million returning Afghan refugees since September 2023, further straining the economy.

China's special representative for Afghanistan told Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi on March 8 that China had contacted Pakistan and was working to reduce tensions. Chinese FM Wang Yi also told his Pakistani counterpart that China 'resolutely supported Pakistan's fight against terrorism' while simultaneously urging a path to reconciliation with the Taliban, illustrating China's complex balancing act.

UN experts formally condemned the Taliban's surging use of corporal punishment in a March 3 press release. The UN Security Council noted Afghanistan's 'alienation from the international community' prevents addressing economic self-sufficiency and counterterrorism commitments. The Taliban's 6-month ban on UN female national personnel continues to impede aid delivery.

relationships.summary: Active armed conflict since February 26, 2026 ('Operation Ghazab Lil Haq'). Pakistan launched airstrikes on Afghan cities including Kabul and Kandahar, citing Taliban harboring of TTP militants. The Taliban launched retaliatory cross-border attacks. Pakistan's defense minister declared 'open war.'

China is a major economic partner, investor in Afghan resources, and diplomatic mediator. Beijing is working to reduce Afghanistan-Pakistan tensions while also supporting Pakistan's counterterrorism stance, maintaining a delicate balance.

India reopened its embassy in Kabul in October 2025 and has pursued partial normalization with the Taliban. Pakistan accuses the Taliban of being an 'Indian proxy,' reflecting its alarm at India's growing engagement with Afghanistan. India conducts trade via Iran's Chahbahar port.

The US accuses the Taliban of 'hostage diplomacy,' has not recognized the Taliban government, and the US ambassador criticized Taliban intransigence at the UN Security Council. US priorities include protecting citizens and mitigating terrorist threats from Afghan territory.

events.summary: Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab Lil Haq on February 26-27, conducting airstrikes on Afghan cities including Kabul, Kandahar, Paktia, and border provinces, in response to Taliban cross-border attacks on Pakistani military positions. Pakistan's Defense Minister declared 'open war' with Afghanistan. By March 13-15, Pakistan continued airstrikes on Kabul, Kandahar, and multiple eastern provinces, claiming over 641 Taliban killed.

India placed its army on high alert in Kashmir following intelligence warnings that 1,000-1,500 Pakistan-backed terror agents could attempt to infiltrate Jammu and Kashmir through the Line of Control. Groups linked to Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed were reportedly regrouping. Indian security forces neutralized three Pakistan-linked Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorists in Kishtwar, Jammu and Kashmir.

Pakistan's security situation was framed by Chatham House as an 'open war' requiring direct de-escalation between Kabul and Islamabad, as the world was distracted by the Iran conflict. Pakistan faces a two-front challenge: western border war with Afghanistan and residual tensions with India on the eastern border. A Pakistani security official stated Pakistan was 'in no hurry to end Operation Ghazab Lil Haq.'

Pakistan's Defence Minister warned the Iran conflict could create a 'Taliban-India-Israel nexus' posing new security challenges for Pakistan. Pakistan accused the Taliban of being an 'Indian proxy' and claimed India had been providing support to the Taliban and TTP. Pakistan's Army Chief met with US Secretary of State Rubio at the Munich Security Conference, emphasizing 'counterterrorism collaboration.'

Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir participated in the Munich Security Conference in February 2026, meeting military leaders from Europe to discuss security challenges. The US highlighted Pakistan's 'significant position' in its strategic framework for Muslim-majority allies alongside Turkey and Indonesia. Pakistan continued intelligence-based counterterrorism operations against TTP militants inside Pakistani territory.

relationships.summary: Active armed conflict since late February 2026. Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab Lil Haq with airstrikes across Afghanistan including Kabul and Kandahar, citing Taliban harboring of TTP militants responsible for attacks inside Pakistan. The Taliban launched retaliatory cross-border operations.

Post-Operation Sindoor (May 2025 four-day conflict), relations remain highly tense. Pakistan accuses India of supporting TTP and the Taliban as a proxy. Indian Army is on high alert in Kashmir amid infiltration warnings. Both countries remain nuclear-armed and on hair-trigger alert.

China is Pakistan's closest strategic partner and top arms supplier, providing air defense systems used in the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict. China 'resolutely supports Pakistan's fight against terrorism' per FM Wang Yi and is working to mediate the Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict.

The US-Pakistan relationship has been cautiously rebuilt. Joint CT exercises (Inspired Gambit 2026) continue and US views Pakistan as a key partner for South Asian stability. US mediated the May 2025 India-Pakistan ceasefire. Pakistan highlighted by US Ambassador as central to Muslim-majority alliance network.

events.summary: India's Union Cabinet approved the first major relaxation of Press Note 3 (2020), which had restricted Chinese investment in India, allowing global funds with minor Chinese ownership to invest and enabling faster approvals for select technology partnerships. This was paired with India's defence sector pivoting from heavy hardware to high-tech electronics, sensors, and software capabilities.

Indian army was placed on high alert in Jammu and Kashmir following intelligence warnings that 1,000-1,500 Pakistan-backed militants linked to Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed could attempt cross-LoC infiltration. Three Pakistan-linked JeM terrorists were neutralized in a joint operation in Kishtwar, Jammu and Kashmir. India rebuffed Pakistan's claims at the UN Human Rights Council regarding J&K.

India raised its defence budget by 15.3% to Rs 7.84 lakh crore ($88.5 billion) for FY2026-27, the largest increase in years, driven by lessons from Operation Sindoor (May 2025 conflict with Pakistan). The budget emphasized 'Make in India' defense manufacturing, with Rs 2.19 lakh crore for capital outlay. India's defense exports hit a record Rs 23,622 crore in FY2024-25, up 34 times from a decade ago.

India projected 7.4% GDP growth for FY2025-26, though growth was expected to decelerate slightly in FY2026-27 due to 50% US tariffs on Indian exports under President Trump. India's budget raised capital expenditure 9% to Rs 12.2 trillion ($133.1 billion). India's BBC budget analysis noted it is pushing domestic manufacturing amid rising global geopolitical tensions including the Iran war.

India planned to ease foreign direct investment rules in its defense sector, raising the automatic route FDI cap from 49% to 74% to attract majority foreign ownership. The reform was designed to motivate defense partner nations' companies to invest in Indian firms following the May 2025 Pakistan conflict. India's defense ministry requested a 20% increase in spending for FY2026-27.

relationships.summary: Highly tense following the four-day Operation Sindoor conflict (May 7-10, 2025), the first nuclear-armed nation drone war. India placed on high alert in Kashmir over infiltration threats. Pakistan accuses India of supporting the Taliban and TTP against Pakistan. India rejects all claims and continues counter-terrorism operations in J&K.

India-China relations are in cautious diplomatic reset following August 2025 border talks agreeing to peaceful management of the LAC, resumption of direct flights, border trade, and next round of boundary talks to be held in China in 2026. Infrastructure race continues along the LAC. India easing some Chinese FDI restrictions.

India reopened its Kabul embassy in October 2025 and is pursuing partial normalization with the Taliban government. India trades with Afghanistan via Chahbahar port in Iran. Pakistan alleges India is using the Taliban as a proxy, which India denies.

The US mediated the India-Pakistan ceasefire in May 2025. US-India defense and technology cooperation is deepening, though Trump's 50% tariffs on Indian exports have created economic friction. India is part of the US strategic framework alongside Turkey and Pakistan in Muslim-majority ally networks.

events.summary: A drone strike by RSF forces south of Khartoum targeted a secondary school and a hospital, killing seventeen civilians, most of them students. The attack came as SAF forces continued to make battlefield gains in Kordofan, and amid international calls for a ceasefire. This strike was among approximately 198 drone strikes documented by ACLED in just the first two months of 2026.

SAF forces captured Bara, the second-largest city in North Kordofan state, following a barrage of airstrikes and troop movements. The advance consolidated the military government's position in the state capital El-Obeid and opened supply routes toward Khartoum. The SAF has been methodically pressing RSF forces out of the Kordofan corridor since early 2026.

The UN Security Council sanctioned four senior RSF commanders, including the brother of RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, imposing travel bans and asset freezes. The UNSC issued a statement expressing grave concern over deteriorating security in Kordofan and Darfur, condemning drone strikes on civilians and humanitarian workers. The sanctions marked the first formal UNSC punitive action specifically targeting RSF leadership.

Sudan's civil war passed 1,000 days of fighting as the UN Security Council held an emergency session, with Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo warning of a 'genocidal path' following the RSF's capture and siege of El Fasher. An independent UN fact-finding mission described atrocities committed by the RSF in North Darfur as bearing indicators of genocide, with at least 6,000 killed in and around El Fasher. More than 30 million people require humanitarian assistance in what the UN describes as the world's largest hunger crisis.

relationships.summary: Sudan's SAF government has repeatedly accused the UAE of supplying weapons, drones, and logistical support to the RSF. Sudan's Foreign Minister stated SAF forces are fighting 'foreign interference.' The Sudanese government severed ties with the UAE and demanded its envoy's expulsion. The UAE has denied supporting the RSF, but independent investigations, including by the New York Times and Reuters, documented Emirati supply convoys.

Egypt has emerged as a key SAF backer, reportedly operating Turkish-made Bayraktar combat drones from a remote airstrip near the Egyptian-Sudanese border to strike RSF supply convoys. Egypt is part of the 'Quad' mediation framework (with Saudi Arabia, UAE, and the US) seeking a ceasefire, though Cairo's direct military involvement complicates its mediator role.

Saudi Arabia is a key member of the Quad mediation framework pushing for a humanitarian truce. Riyadh has publicly condemned RSF attacks on civilians and humanitarian convoys. Saudi Arabia's motivations include countering UAE influence in the Horn of Africa and preserving regional stability critical to its Vision 2030 economic program.

Chad has hosted nearly 1 million Sudanese refugees and faced direct military incursions. The RSF killed seven Chadian soldiers in January 2026 in a cross-border incident, prompting Chad to close its entire 1,400-km border with Sudan in February 2026. Chad is accused by the SAF of facilitating UAE arms shipments to the RSF through its territory, allegations the Chadian government denies.

US envoy Massad Boulos has described himself as 'cautiously optimistic' about achieving a humanitarian ceasefire. Washington has threatened sanctions on actors obstructing a peace deal and has designated Sudanese Islamist factions affiliated with the SAF as terrorist organizations in March 2026, complicating the Quad mediation framework.

events.summary: Devastating landslides in southern Ethiopia's Gamo Zone killed at least 125 people, displacing more than 11,000. The landslides, triggered by heavy rains, struck multiple areas over several days. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed visited the scene on Saturday to offer condolences and pledge government support, as rescue efforts continued.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed declared there would be 'no war' in the embattled Tigray region, speaking in the Tigrayan language, and asserted that Addis Ababa 'continues to believe problems should be resolved only through dialogue.' The statement came as troops and artillery were reportedly massing on both sides of the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, with analysts warning war could be imminent.

Despite Eritrea's past cooperation with Ethiopia during the Tigray war, tensions between Asmara and Addis Ababa have reached a new peak, with both countries reportedly moving troops toward the border. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of supporting dissident TPLF factions and fomenting the Amhara insurgency, while Eritrea fears Ethiopia's stated ambition to seize Eritrean Red Sea port access. Civilian residents in northern Ethiopia described covert Eritrean troop movements.

Clashes erupted in Tigray's Tselemti district between Tigrayan forces and Ethiopian federal troops in late January, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to cancel all flights to the region for several days. TPLF-aligned forces briefly captured the towns of Alamata and Korem in Southern Tigray before withdrawing. The clashes represented the most serious breakdown of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement since its signing, with the TPLF claiming Ethiopian drone strikes targeted their fighters.

relationships.summary: Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated sharply, threatening to reignite full-scale war. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of supporting dissident TPLF factions and arming Amhara rebels (50,000 rounds of ammunition allegedly intercepted in January 2026). Eritrea fears Ethiopia will seek to forcibly seize port access at Assab or Massawa. Both countries have mobilized forces to the border.

Following Turkish mediation in late 2024 and the Ankara Declaration, Ethiopia and Somalia restored diplomatic relations in January 2025 and renewed an agreement for 2,500 Ethiopian troops to serve in AUSSOM (the AU peacekeeping mission in Somalia). However, Somalia later canceled its agreement with the UAE over Somaliland recognition, creating regional ripple effects that impacted Ethiopia's diplomatic environment.

Sudan's SAF has accused Ethiopia of hosting an RSF training camp in the Benishangul-Gumuz region near the border. SAF officials also allege that RSF supply routes transit through western Ethiopia with Emirati involvement. The ICDI reported that a new war front in Blue Nile state was partly attributed to RSF attacks backed by Ethiopia, though these claims remain disputed.

events.summary: US Africa Command (AFRICOM), in coordination with the Federal Government of Somalia, conducted an airstrike targeting al-Shabaab on March 11. A separate US strike targeting ISIS-Somalia was conducted on March 8. These strikes are part of an intensifying US military campaign in Somalia under Trump administration policy.

Somalia's armed forces reported gaining ground against al-Shabaab in the Middle Shabelle region, seizing one of the group's strategic holdouts. The advance was part of Operation Rolling Thunder, a joint operation with Ugandan African Union troops launched earlier in March. Al-Shabaab's territorial control has declined in some areas but the group continues to conduct sophisticated attacks and controls approximately 30% of Somalia's territory.

Somalia's Somali Future Council warned of political 'instability' if elections are delayed, noting that the Federal Parliament's mandate expires April 14 and the President's term ends May 15, 2026. The warning drew parallels to the 2021 political crisis when election disputes triggered armed clashes in Mogadishu. Persistent disagreements over the electoral model and constitutional amendments have deepened political uncertainty.

Kenya and Somalia announced their shared border will reopen in April 2026, nearly 15 years after it was closed due to al-Shabaab regional attacks. Kenyan President William Ruto said troops would be deployed alongside the border opening for extra security. The announcement followed diplomatic normalization between the two countries and was tied to broader regional security cooperation agreements.

relationships.summary: The US has intensified military operations in Somalia under Trump administration policy, conducting dozens of airstrikes against both al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia (in Puntland). A US weapons delivery of undisclosed value was made to the Somali government in February 2026. Civilian casualty concerns have been raised by local human rights organizations. The US also delivered military assistance to bolster Somali army operations.

Somalia terminated all agreements with the UAE in January 2026, including port operations and security cooperation deals, following Israel's recognition of Somaliland and the transit of a pro-UAE separatist figure through Somali airspace. The UAE had been conducting airstrikes against ISIS-Somalia in Puntland with US support. The breakdown represents a significant diplomatic rupture with major implications for counterterrorism cooperation.

Kenya and Somalia agreed to reopen their shared border in April 2026, nearly 15 years after its closure. Nairobi will deploy security forces alongside the reopening. Al-Shabaab has continued to conduct cross-border attacks in northeastern Kenya, most recently killing a local chief and teacher in January 2026, partly to pressure Kenya to withdraw from AUSSOM peacekeeping.

events.summary: Both the DRC government and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels accused each other of violating ceasefire terms, while active fighting continued in North Kivu around the Rubaya coltan mine. DRC and Rwandan forces exchanged drone and artillery fire, and ceasefire monitoring mechanisms remained unimplemented. The Washington Post reported ongoing clashes on March 13 threatening a fragile peace process.

The United States sanctioned Rwanda's military and four of its top officials for backing M23 rebels in the DRC, marking the first formal US sanctions on Rwanda since the conflict escalated. Rwanda's government said the sanctions 'misrepresented the reality' of the conflict. The sanctions came as the US mediated the Washington Peace Accords between the DRC and Rwanda, which M23 is resisting.

Congolese forces killed Willy Ngoma, the M23 rebel group's military spokesman and senior commander, in a drone strike near the Rubaya coltan mine in North Kivu. The high-profile killing came as FARDC launched a coordinated offensive alongside Wazalendo militia fighters, conducting multiple drone strikes on M23 positions. M23 retaliated with drone attacks against FARDC's Kisangani military command center.

M23 rebels established a parallel administration, taxation system, and judicial structures in eastern DRC territories under their control, according to a UN expert report. M23's occupation force of over 7,000 fighters — including former Congolese army soldiers and allied militias — effectively controls Goma (captured January 2025) and Bukavu (captured February 2025). One year after Goma's fall, all banks remain closed and humanitarian agencies report severely disrupted operations.

relationships.summary: Rwanda is the primary backer of M23, having deployed 3,000–4,000 troops to eastern DRC during peak operations. The US sanctioned Rwanda's military in March 2026 for this support. Rwanda denies direct involvement but the UN, HRW, and independent analysts have documented Rwandan military integration with M23. DRC-Rwanda relations are at their lowest point since the 1990s.

The US is mediating the 'Washington Peace Accords' between DRC and Rwanda, while simultaneously sanctioning Rwanda for obstructing the peace process. The DRC has offered the Rubaya coltan mine to US investors as leverage to attract American engagement. Trump's team has expressed interest in DRC's critical minerals (coltan, cobalt), creating complex US diplomatic incentives.

Qatar is leading the Doha mediation process between the DRC government and M23 rebels, separate from the US-led Washington Accords track. The Doha process produced several non-binding ceasefire agreements in 2025 and established frameworks for a ceasefire verification mechanism, though implementation has repeatedly stalled due to mutual accusations of violations.

Angolan President João Lourenço brokered an ad hoc ceasefire agreement between DRC President Tshisekedi and M23 on February 9, 2026, with the ceasefire nominally taking effect on February 18. Lourenço has served as the African Union's primary mediator in the conflict. However, both sides have accused the other of violating the ceasefire within days of it taking effect.

events.summary: The UN Security Council warned Libya will 'explode again' without political progress, with UNSMIL chief Hanna Serwaa Tetteh reporting 'no meaningful progress' on electoral framework legislation between the rival House of Representatives and High Council of State. Tetteh warned the deadlock has 'further eroded the credibility of both institutions.' The Security Council session also condemned the killing of Saif al-Islam Gaddafi as a 'blatant act of violence' threatening the political transition.

Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, son of slain dictator Muammar Gaddafi and potential challenger in any future Libyan election, was shot dead by four assailants at his compound in Zintan. No group has claimed responsibility. Chatham House analysts noted the killing removes a potential electoral competitor for both the GNU-aligned Dabaiba government in Tripoli and the Haftar family in the east, though it could spark retribution from Gaddafi loyalists.

Armed factions aligned with the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity clashed in the western city of Zawiya, with forces from the Stability Support Apparatus seizing positions held by forces loyal to Prime Minister Dbeibah. The clashes involved heavy weapons. The Red Crescent urged civilians to stay indoors. The incident underscored the fragmented militia landscape in western Libya, where multiple armed factions nominally supporting the same government compete for territory.

Libya's chief military commander, General Mohammed Ali Ahmed al-Haddad, and four other senior Libyan military officials died when their plane crashed near Ankara, Turkey, while returning from official talks with Turkish counterparts. Turkish authorities investigated the crash and found no immediate evidence of foul play, though the deaths created a leadership vacuum in the GNU's military command at a critical juncture.

relationships.summary: Turkey is the primary military backer of the Tripoli-based GNU, having signed a 2019 maritime boundary treaty granting Turkey de facto veto power over Libya's western security sector. Turkish military advisers, drones, and naval assets underpin the GNU's military posture. Turkey has also mediated politically between GNU and eastern factions.

Russia has formally taken over from the Wagner Group in eastern Libya through the Ministry of Defense's Africa Corps, controlling airbases, logistics hubs, and key desert routes toward the Sahel. Russian forces are positioned near critical oil fields in Haftar-controlled eastern Libya. Russia's presence complicates UN mediation efforts and UNSMIL's political roadmap.

The UAE backs Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army (LNA) in eastern Libya, providing funding, drones, and diplomatic support. UAE investment interest in Libya's GNU government has also grown, including Gulf sovereign wealth fund discussions about the Misrata Free Zone. The UAE's dual engagement with both sides reflects its energy and strategic interests in Libya's oil sector.

Italy has maintained engagement with both Libyan factions due to critical energy and migration interests. Italy's Foreign Minister signed a $2.7 billion investment agreement with Qatar to expand the Misrata Free Zone Port. Italy views Libya as key to its energy security (ENI operates major Libyan gas fields) and to managing irregular migration across the Mediterranean.

events.summary: Nigerian troops repelled Boko Haram and ISWAP attacks on two military positions in Borno State, supported by close air support from the Nigerian Air Force. The attacks targeted positions at Azer Bridge (Sector 2) and Banky (Sector 1) in the early hours of March 13. The military stated that soldiers launched coordinated counterattacks that disrupted insurgent formations and forced them to retreat.

ISWAP and Boko Haram (JAS) killed more than 100 Nigerian soldiers in a single week across Borno State in the deadliest seven-day period since the 2018 Metele massacre. Coordinated attacks overran military bases at Konduga, Mainok, Jakana, Marte, Sambisa Forest, Banki Junction, and Kukawa. Two Lieutenant Colonels were among those killed. ISWAP simultaneously attacked four bases in a single night, suggesting reconstituted theatre-level command capacity.

President Tinubu declared that Nigeria will defeat terrorism and banditry, describing the threats as 'unacceptable' at the Second National Economic Council Conference. Tinubu announced plans for seven zones of mechanization and committed to strengthening security forces, while commending governors in Borno, Katsina, and Kaduna. The announcement came amid persistent criticism that the military has been repeatedly unable to protect civilian populations despite forewarning.

JNIM (Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin) claimed its first attack in Nigeria in 2025 and has threatened to push south toward the Gulf of Guinea. In early February 2026, jihadists killed nearly 170 people in western Nigeria's Kwara State in the country's deadliest attack of the year. The attack reflected the spread of Sahel-based extremism into Nigeria's northwest and Middle Belt regions, previously dominated by banditry rather than ideological insurgency.

relationships.summary: An initial contingent of approximately 100 US military personnel arrived in Nigeria in February 2026 to provide non-combat technical advice and intelligence support, with several hundred more expected. Tinubu described the US alliance as 'strategic, focused on protecting vulnerable communities, and operationally led by Nigerian troops.' AFRICOM continues intelligence-sharing and drone surveillance operations targeting jihadist networks in the Lake Chad Basin.

Nigeria and Cameroon cooperate through the Multinational Joint Task Force (MNJTF) targeting Boko Haram and ISWAP in the Lake Chad Basin. Cameroonian authorities arrested two suspected ISWAP militants who fled across the border from Nigeria in March 2026. However, the MNJTF's operational effectiveness has declined as the Sahel juntas (Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso) withdrew their contributions.

Niger's junta government has effectively ceased security cooperation with Nigeria. The ACLED documented a sharp increase in Islamic extremism in the tri-border region encompassing northwestern Nigeria, northern Benin, and southeastern Niger. JNIM has exploited the collapse of regional security cooperation to expand into this previously less-affected area, threatening coastal West African states.

events.summary: JNIM continued its months-long fuel blockade of Bamako, intercepting convoys from Ivory Coast and Senegal since September 2025. HRW documented the January 2026 execution of a dozen truck drivers by JNIM militants enforcing the blockade, which it characterized as violations of international human rights law. Popular unrest in Bamako grew at the junta's inability to break the blockade, which has caused severe economic disruption.

The US State Department said it would lift sanctions on top Malian junta officials as part of a deal to allow Washington to surveil and combat jihadist groups in the Sahel, including JNIM, which is believed to be holding an abducted American citizen. The offer reflected Washington's pragmatic recalibration toward the Mali junta despite its expulsion of French and UN forces and its partnership with Russia's Africa Corps.

JNIM conducted a large-scale coordinated offensive across the central Sahel into Benin in February, with Burkina Faso as the main battleground. In Mali, JNIM has consolidated control of northern and central territory while sustaining the Bamako fuel blockade. Russia's Africa Corps replaced the Wagner Group, which formally withdrew in June 2025, but analysts say the force transition has not improved Malian security.

Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger launched the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) Unified Force, a 6,000-strong joint military force headquartered in Niamey, at the December 2025 summit. The force represents the third attempt by Sahel states to establish a joint security mechanism. The AES nations also jointly voted against a UN General Assembly ceasefire resolution on Ukraine, signaling a definitive diplomatic break from France and Western institutions.

relationships.summary: Russia's Africa Corps (successor to Wagner Group, which formally withdrew in June 2025) remains Mali's primary security partner, conducting joint combat operations with Malian forces against JNIM and Tuareg rebels. Russia supplies military equipment including drones and armored vehicles. Despite this partnership, analysts note that Russian-backed forces have failed to contain JNIM's expansion or break its siege of Bamako.

Mali expelled French forces in 2022 after the military coup. France has since pivoted to an Algeria-based surveillance approach to monitor Sahel jihadist groups. Mali is part of the AES bloc that has systematically expelled French and UN forces, expelled the MINUSMA peacekeeping mission, and aligned diplomatically with Russia. France has largely disengaged from direct Malian security.

Mali and Burkina Faso are core AES partners with close alignment on security, political, and economic cooperation. Both face JNIM insurgencies, rely on Russian security assistance, and have jointly expelled Western forces. The AES Unified Force launched in December 2025 represents their deepest military integration to date, though the force has yet to demonstrate decisive operational impact.

events.summary: HRW documented that JNIM killed at least 38 civilians, abducted 9 women, and burned property in three separate incidents in northeastern Burkina Faso since late January 2026. On February 14, JNIM executed at least 34 civilians and burned the Titao market in the North region; on February 22, JNIM fighters executed four shopkeepers in Manni. The attacks targeted communities with perceived ties to the military's volunteer militia (VDPs).

Explosions were heard near the presidential palace in Ouagadougou on the night of February 28 to March 1, 2026, triggering speculation about an internal coup attempt. The government denied a coup, attributing the incident to a vehicle fire. However, multiple sources suggest the incident reflected internal tensions within the military, with officers summoned to Ouagadougou reportedly refusing to comply — a sign of dissent against Captain Ibrahim Traoré's leadership.

JNIM conducted more than 30 coordinated attacks in Burkina Faso in February, part of a region-wide offensive following a senior JNIM commander's defection to the Islamic State Sahel Province. The offensive killed more than 120 soldiers, forest guards, and VDP fighters, with the deadliest incident at Titao killing approximately 80 security personnel. Reuters reported diplomatic sources describing 'unprecedented coordination' among the militants.

The military junta dissolved all political parties by decree, with Interior Minister Emile Zerbo stating it was part of an effort to 'rebuild the state.' The decree effectively abolished all 100+ registered political parties, with their assets transferred to the state. The move followed years of suspended political activity after the 2022 coup and was seen as consolidating Captain Ibrahim Traoré's grip on power amid escalating jihadist pressure.

relationships.summary: Burkina Faso has aligned with Russia for security training and equipment. Unlike Mali, Russia's Africa Corps engagement in Burkina Faso is limited to training rather than direct combat operations. Burkina Faso has expelled French forces and ECOWAS peacekeepers in favor of Russian partnerships. The AES bloc collectively procures weapons from Russia, Turkey, Iran, and China.

Burkina Faso and Mali are the closest partners in the AES bloc, sharing contiguous border areas where JNIM freely operates. The two countries participate in joint military operations and share intelligence through the AES Unified Force framework. Both face nearly identical security challenges from JNIM's expansion and have adopted nearly identical political postures rejecting Western influence.

France was expelled from Burkina Faso in February 2023 after the second military coup. Relations remain hostile, with the junta blocking French media (BBC, VOA) and NGOs. France has announced a new monitoring-from-Algeria strategy for the Sahel rather than direct engagement. Former Burkina Faso president Paul-Henri Damiba was arrested in Togo in January 2026 over an alleged coup plot against Traoré.

events.summary: Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) attacked the Tahoua air base (Air Base 401) in western Niger in its second attack on Nigerien air infrastructure after the January 29 assault on Niamey's Dori Hamani International Airport and Airbase 101. The attackers then assaulted the 42nd Combined Arms Battalion headquarters near Tahoua. The attacks are part of a systematic ISSP campaign to degrade Niger's air surveillance and transport capabilities.

Nigerien President Abdourahamane Tchiani announced a détente in tensions with Algeria ahead of renewed progress on the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline project, nearly a year after AES countries recalled ambassadors from Algeria over a drone controversy. The diplomatic reset was driven by economic necessity as the pipeline represents a critical revenue opportunity for Niger. France simultaneously announced a new Algeria-based surveillance strategy for the Sahel.

A Nigerien military drone strike targeting three Islamic State militants in western Niger killed at least 17 civilians, including four children. HRW stated the strike could amount to war crimes. The incident reflected the chronic problem of civilian casualties from aerial counterinsurgency operations across the Sahel, even as the Nigerien military relies increasingly on drones to compensate for limited ground force capacity.

IS Sahel Province fighters used armed drones, small arms, and mortars to assault Dori Hamani International Airport and military Airbase 101 in a two-hour battle. The base houses Nigerien military drone operations and serves as headquarters for the Alliance of Sahel States. All attackers were killed or captured, but analysts described the assault as a 'deliberate, high-value operation' meant to degrade Niger's strategic military infrastructure.

relationships.summary: Russia's Africa Corps provides training to Nigerien security forces, though at lower levels than in Mali. Niger expelled US forces (completing withdrawal by mid-2024) and French forces, creating a security vacuum that Russia has partially filled. The AES Unified Force launched in December 2025 is headquartered in Niamey, reflecting Niger's central role in the bloc's collective defense architecture.

After a year-long diplomatic rupture over a drone controversy, Niger and Algeria are cautiously re-engaging, driven partly by the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline project. Algeria provides a transit route for hydrocarbon exports critical to Niger's economy. Algeria has sought to position itself as a regional security partner for the Sahel states, offering an alternative to both Western and Russian dependency.

Relations between Niger and Nigeria have deteriorated since the 2023 coup. ECOWAS threatened military intervention, which Niger and its AES partners labeled a 'declaration of war.' Nigeria hosted the ECOWAS standby force during the standoff but did not intervene. Cross-border jihadist violence in the Nigeria-Niger-Benin tri-border zone has intensified, complicating any bilateral security cooperation.

events.summary: Rwanda warned it may withdraw its troops from Mozambique's insurgency-hit Cabo Delgado province, citing insufficient international recognition of its substantial military investment. Rwanda deployed forces in 2021 at Mozambique's request and has been central to counterinsurgency operations. The warning came amid tensions with the international community over Rwanda's DRC involvement, creating pressure on Kigali to reconsider its deployments.

ACLED documented continued fighting in Cabo Delgado's Catupa forest following a large Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) ambush on a commercial convoy on February 22. ISM deployed an estimated 300 fighters in the ambush, looting a truckload of rice destined for the group's Namurussia base. State forces including Mozambican army, police, and Rwandan Mi-24 attack helicopters engaged ISM over several days, but ISM retained control of Catupa forest and the strategic N380 road.

ISM fighters were observed moving south from Macomia district toward Quissanga and Ancuabe districts, with one group approaching an artisanal gold mine at Muaja, causing miners to flee. The FADM navy established a 'no-sail' zone along the Macomia coast, firing warning shots at a fishing boat near Luchete village. ISM's southward movement threatens to expand the conflict beyond its traditional Cabo Delgado heartland.

TotalEnergies' $20 billion LNG project at Afungi remains suspended, with its deadline pushed back from 2024 to at least 2030 due to continuous ISM attacks in the surrounding area. Nearly 60,000 people fled violence in July–August 2025, and 90% of internally displaced persons are women, elderly, or disabled. Over half of Cabo Delgado's health facilities are destroyed or damaged, constituting one of Africa's worst ongoing humanitarian emergencies.

relationships.summary: Rwanda deployed forces to Cabo Delgado in 2021 at Mozambique's request and has been the most effective external military partner in the counterinsurgency, operating Mi-24 helicopters, conducting joint patrols, and taking the fight to ISM strongholds. However, Rwanda's threat to withdraw its troops in March 2026, driven by frustration over international criticism of its DRC actions, creates significant risk for Mozambique's security.

South Africa contributed forces to the SADC Mission in Mozambique (SAMIM), which conducted counterinsurgency operations in Cabo Delgado from 2021. South African Special Forces have conducted joint operations with Mozambican troops. SAMIM has gradually reduced its footprint as security improved in some areas, though ISM retains capabilities in Catupa forest and is conducting southward probing attacks.

TotalEnergies' suspended $20 billion LNG project at Afungi represents France's most direct stake in Mozambique's stability. The project has been on hold since the 2021 Palma attack and the project deadline has been pushed back repeatedly to at least 2030. TotalEnergies is monitoring security conditions for any potential restart of operations, which would require a significant and durable improvement in Cabo Delgado.

events.summary: Chad closed its entire 1,400-kilometer border with Sudan 'until further notice' after RSF fighters crossed into Chadian territory during fighting for the border town of Tina, killing five Chadian soldiers and three civilians and wounding 12 others. The closure severed critical humanitarian corridors used to supply food and medicine to Darfur, affecting nearly 1 million Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad. The government described it as a response to 'repeated incursions and violations' by Sudanese warring parties.

Chad now hosts over 900,000 Sudanese refugees — the most per capita of any African country — and is itself facing a severe humanitarian crisis with 40% of its own population requiring assistance. The UN released its 2026 Humanitarian Action Plan for Chad, noting the number of people in need decreased by 42% but remains high. Boko Haram and its affiliates continue to drive insecurity in the Lake Chad Basin, displacing over 250,000 people.

Chadian President Mahamat Idriss Déby visited Paris and met with French President Macron to agree on a 'revitalised partnership' focused on economic cooperation rather than military ties. The meeting came after Chad abruptly expelled French troops in November 2024, ending nearly 80 years of continuous French military presence. The Elysée noted 'economic and cultural dynamics have now replaced security dynamics' as the frame for bilateral relations.

The RSF killed seven Chadian soldiers in a cross-border attack in mid-January 2026, which the RSF claimed was an inadvertent pursuit of Sudanese Armed Forces fighters into Chadian territory. Chadian officials described the attack as 'premeditated.' The incident strained RSF-Chad relations and prompted Chadian security officials to internally criticize President Déby's policy of allowing UAE weapons shipments to the RSF to transit through Chadian territory.

relationships.summary: Chad shares a 1,400-km border with Sudan and has been directly impacted by the conflict, hosting nearly 1 million refugees. Chad is accused by the SAF of facilitating UAE weapons shipments to the RSF through Chadian territory. The RSF's killing of seven Chadian soldiers in January and the subsequent cross-border fighting in Tina in February prompted Chad to close its border. Chad officially claims neutrality but faces internal divisions over the policy.

The UAE has become a major investor in Chad's economy through its Connexion 2030 development plan. However, Chad's facilitation of UAE weapons shipments to the RSF has created domestic political tension, particularly among the Zaghawa community to which President Déby belongs — a community that has faced RSF atrocities in Darfur. Chad is reportedly reconsidering the extent of this transit arrangement under US pressure.

After expelling French military forces in November 2024, Chad and France are pursuing a 'revitalised' economic partnership following Déby's January 2026 Paris visit. France remains Chad's leading bilateral development partner. The military rupture was driven partly by Chadian perceptions that France was too critical of its ties to the UAE and RSF. France seeks a foothold in the Sahel after its expulsions from Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.

Chad participates in the Multinational Joint Task Force (MNJTF) with Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon, and Benin to combat Boko Haram and ISWAP in the Lake Chad Basin.
